edges.effect_quant: The strongest quantitative studies point in a harmful direction, but the pooled magnitude varies across populations and methods.
edges.population: adults with frequent high-temperature meat intake
edges.mechanism: High-temperature cooking forms heterocyclic amines and PAHs that can damage colonic DNA after metabolic activation.
edges.summary: For colorectal cancer, the most useful starting point is the 2018 Zhang cohort in Mutat Res. It found that high- temperature meat cooking tracks with higher risk or worse outcomes, and the follow-on evidence is broadly consistent even when absolute benefit or harm is modest.
edges.caveats: Residual confounding and reverse causation remain possible in some observational studies, so the main readout is direction and plausibility rather than one exact risk number.

evidence.notes: The Adenomatous Polyposis Coli (APC) mutation spectra in different anatomical regions of the large intestine in colorectal cancer.
